messages.author: edd4914c326b6d31
messages.subject: rstan: some choices of defaults
parts:
traceplot(sf), where sf is a stanfit object, flashes all the plots up
without waiting. This is not what I expected, based partly on coda's
behavior. I see there is a parameter that controls this, but perhaps a
different default would be appropriate.

Earlier I was surprised when
x <- monitor(extract(r4, permuted=FALSE, inc_warmup = TRUE))
(rf a stanfit object) printed the results. Again, there is a parameter
to control the behavior, but this seems an odd default. I don't even
think printing should be an option. There already is a print command,
which seems to produce the same information, and someone who wants to
see the results can also do
monitor(extract(r4, permuted=FALSE, inc_warmup = TRUE))
and see them.

This is with the development version.

messages.author: 8aa9b8cc06fdc99c
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] rstan: some choices of defaults
parts:
On 9/17/13 5:13 PM, Ross Boylan wrote:
> traceplot(sf), where sf is a stanfit object, flashes all the plots up
> without waiting. This is not what I expected, based partly on coda's
> behavior. I see there is a parameter that controls this, but perhaps a
> different default would be appropriate.

What does Coda do and/or what would you like Stan to do?

I usually only do that by mistake, but if I have something
like a huge IRT model then I have to wait forever for
them all to print, which is definitely inconvenient (and
probably wasteful of memory).

You can scroll back through the plots using command+(left arrow),
but that doesn't help much if there are too many of them.

One option would be to do something like ask you if you
realize this is going to draw a gazillion plots. I think it'd
also be handy if there was a way to pull out a subset of plots.
So if I have a parameter theta[N] where N=1000, I pretty much
am never going to want to see all 1000 thrown up. What I
would like to be able to do is

traceplot(fit,"theta[1:10]")

or something like that.

> Earlier I was surprised when
> x <- monitor(extract(r4, permuted=FALSE, inc_warmup = TRUE))
> (rf a stanfit object) printed the results.

> Again, there is a parameter
> to control the behavior, but this seems an odd default.
Agreed.

> I don't even
> think printing should be an option.

I agree.

Jiqiang --- or anyone --- is there a reason RStan does it the way
it does it? If not, I think this is a good change assuming
the following is right about print. I've never used monitor()
myself.

> There already is a print command,
> which seems to produce the same information, and someone who wants to
> see the results can also do
> monitor(extract(r4, permuted=FALSE, inc_warmup = TRUE))
> and see them.
>
> This is with the development version.

Thanks for the version heads up. There's still a bit of
time before the 2.0 beta, but we are knocking down the pull
requests that are outstanding pretty quickly now that the model
tests are all ship shape.

- Bob

messages.author: edd4914c326b6d31
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] rstan: some choices of defaults
parts:
On Tue, Sep 17, 2013 at 08:10:06PM -0400, Bob Carpenter wrote:
>
>
> On 9/17/13 5:13 PM, Ross Boylan wrote:
>> traceplot(sf), where sf is a stanfit object, flashes all the plots up
>> without waiting. This is not what I expected, based partly on coda's
>> behavior. I see there is a parameter that controls this, but perhaps a
>> different default would be appropriate.
>
> What does Coda do and/or what would you like Stan to do?

Coda displays the first screenful of plots and then pauses until you click on it.

Somehow coda, or more likely the R graphic system, knows if the
display is a terminal or not; if output is going to a pdf it just
prints everything to the file.

This doesn't solve the problem of having too many plots but at least
it lets you see a few of them. I think I C-c in the terminal when
I've seen enough.

An idea I like even better appears below.

>
> I usually only do that by mistake, but if I have something
> like a huge IRT model then I have to wait forever for
> them all to print, which is definitely inconvenient (and
> probably wasteful of memory).
>
> You can scroll back through the plots using command+(left arrow),
> but that doesn't help much if there are too many of them.
>
> One option would be to do something like ask you if you
> realize this is going to draw a gazillion plots.

Provided there is a way to interrupt it, that seems like something
that can be left to the user.

Actually, since stan knows about blocks of parameters, maybe it could
just print the first 5 in each block, with an option to override that
(i.e, set the number in each block to display). So in my case plot()
would show the first 5 alpha, the first 5 beta, and the 2 sigma
parameters (and lp__?). That's far from complete, but might be useful

Fancier versions could allow a list of indices, with the list names
matching parameter names.

It's not clear to me such functionality belongs in the package...

>I think it'd
> also be handy if there was a way to pull out a subset of plots.
> So if I have a parameter theta[N] where N=1000, I pretty much
> am never going to want to see all 1000 thrown up. What I
> would like to be able to do is
>
> traceplot(fit,"theta[1:10]")
>
> or something like that.
>

With coda I would compute (by hand) the indices of a subset of
parameters and display them. The results in rstan seem to be a little
more buried--for coda the results are effectively a matrix and I
simply selected columns, whereas in stan I've had to kind of pick
through things. It has matrix output (extract(permuted=FALSE)?) but I
haven't quite gotten the hang of it.

Ross

>
>    traceplot(fit,"theta[1:10]")
>
> or something like that.

In fact, you can do something like the following

traceplot(fit, pars = "theta[1]")
traceplot(fit, pars = c("theta[1]","theta[2]"))

--
Jiqiang

way to optimize it.
